Alternative dose-response curve models

Source: R/fit_curve_models.R
curve_models.Rd

Fit functions for apply_fit, each fitting one curve shape from drc to the averaged response of a single-agent experiment.

Usage

ll3_fit_fn(avg_dt, x_col = "x", conc_col = "Concentration")

ll5_fit_fn(avg_dt, x_col = "x", conc_col = "Concentration")

weibull1_fit_fn(avg_dt, x_col = "x", conc_col = "Concentration")

weibull2_fit_fn(avg_dt, x_col = "x", conc_col = "Concentration")

gompertz_fit_fn(avg_dt, x_col = "x", conc_col = "Concentration")

hormesis_fit_fn(avg_dt, x_col = "x", conc_col = "Concentration")

Arguments

avg_dt

data.table for one drug, cell line and normalization type, as apply_fit supplies it.

x_col

string; the response column.

conc_col

string; the concentration column.

Value

Named list of one row: the model's parameters, then r2, converged, ec50_extrapolated, n_conc and fit_type.

Details

These complement fit_drug_response_metrics, which fits the 4-parameter log-logistic the processing pipeline uses. Reach for one of these when that shape is the wrong one: ll3_fit_fn when a curve is too sparse or too shallow to support four free parameters, ll5_fit_fn, weibull1_fit_fn, weibull2_fit_fn and gompertz_fit_fn when the response is asymmetric, and hormesis_fit_fn for a low-dose stimulation that a log-logistic cannot represent at all.

Each returns the model's own parameters rather than the Metrics schema. Parameters playing the same role across models share the names logisticFit() uses — h for the slope, x_0 and x_inf for the asymptotes, ec50 for the inflection point — and the rest are named for what they are. Write them to an assay of their own: an assay of these is not the Metrics schema, so nothing reading Metrics will understand it.

All of them also return r2, converged, n_conc and fit_type, so two models fitted to the same data can be compared, and ec50_extrapolated, which is TRUE when the fitted ec50 lies outside the concentrations tested. That happens whenever a drug is too weak to reach its own midpoint on the plate: the fit can still be a good one, but the ec50 is not a measurement and should not be read as a potency.

A fit that does not converge returns a row of NA parameters with converged = FALSE, rather than raising. A fit that failed is a result; dropping the cell would make it indistinguishable from one that was never fitted. converged = FALSE also covers a fit that finished on parameters that say nothing about the data: one whose own model cannot evaluate them, and one whose ec50 ran a thousandfold outside the tested concentrations, which happens on a response too flat to have a midpoint.

ec50 is bounded below at a positive value, because every model here evaluates log(dose/ec50) and is undefined without it.

ll3_fit_fn and hormesis_fit_fn fix the lower asymptote at zero, so neither suits a GR-normalized response that goes below it: the model cannot reach the data and the misfit shows up as a poor r2 rather than as a failure.

See also

apply_fit, fit_drug_response_metrics

Examples

dt <- data.frame(Concentration = 10^(-3:3), x = c(1, .98, .9, .5, .2, .1, .08))
ll3_fit_fn(dt)
#> $h
#> [1] 0.6366549
#> 
#> $x_0
#> [1] 1.032444
#> 
#> $ec50
#> [1] 1.127042
#> 
#> $r2
#> [1] 0.9900098
#> 
#> $converged
#> [1] TRUE
#> 
#> $ec50_extrapolated
#> [1] FALSE
#> 
#> $n_conc
#> [1] 7
#> 
#> $fit_type
#> [1] "DRC3pLogLogisticLowerFixed"
#> 
gompertz_fit_fn(dt)
#> $h
#> [1] NA
#> 
#> $x_inf
#> [1] NA
#> 
#> $x_0
#> [1] NA
#> 
#> $ec50
#> [1] NA
#> 
#> $r2
#> [1] NA
#> 
#> $converged
#> [1] FALSE
#> 
#> $ec50_extrapolated
#> [1] NA
#> 
#> $n_conc
#> [1] 7
#> 
#> $fit_type
#> [1] "DRC4pGompertz"
#>
